items_missed: Never confirmed availability for the requested date. She opened by confirming 'your move date is September 26th which falls on a Saturday' but never said 'and we do have availability that day' — the customer has no signal the date is actually holdable, which is the one thing that makes a same-call booking feel urgent. She then steered him off that date to Sunday without ever establishing that Saturday was secured.

No additional-rooms probe — garage, storage unit, balcony, patio never asked. She ran a strong item-by-item inventory of the living space but the question 'is there anything in a garage, a storage unit, or on a balcony we need to grab?' never came, and on an apartment-to-apartment move a balcony set or a storage cage is the most common missed-inventory surprise on move day.
Storage stops and additional stops never asked. Two questions, ten seconds, and neither was put to the customer.

Special considerations never probed beyond walk distance. No narrow hallways, no tight turns, no doorway width — and this is a large sectional couch and an entertainment center coming down from a fourth floor unit through an elevator. Sectional-through-elevator is exactly the item that blows an estimate.

Access concerns thin. She established the elevator exists and measured walk distances well, but never asked whether the elevator has to be reserved, whether either complex requires a COI, or where the truck can actually stage. The customer even told her 'we get our keys next weekend and we'll just need to go and like reconfirm where the closest is for you guys' — an open invitation to set a follow-up on destination access that she closed with 'Wonderful. Yeah, thank you.'

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. Not once — no $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no coverage framing at all. 'Insurance' appeared only as a word inside the what's-included list. The customer named 'care' as his first concern ('I think our biggest thing is like, of course care, right') and it drew a response about budget instead.

Meet Your Mover never mentioned — and the customer's first stated worry was care of his things. The pre-move email with the mover's photo and name is the direct answer to 'who is actually showing up at my door' and it went unused.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned. The customer's second and third stated worries were 'cost and time.' The on-time guarantee is the differentiator that speaks to time and it never came out.

Clock start never explained. She covered the 2.5-hour minimum and fifteen-minute proration in one breath — 'What we have is a two and a half hour minimum. If we go being on two and a half hours, we will prorate the time in every fifteen minute increments' — but never said when the billable clock actually begins or ends. On a move with a thirty-minute drive between addresses, whether drive time is on the clock is the customer's obvious next question and it was left unanswered.

Quote padded above her own stated typical range. She said 'typically a two bedroom apartment, we would just need three and a half, sometimes up to five and a half hours,' then immediately narrowed to 'I would suggest budget for the mid to higher range which is four and a half to five and a half hours just to be on the safe side.' The inventory she just took is a bed, a dresser, a sectional, an entertainment center, a dog crate, two desks, two TVs, two display cabinets and under twenty boxes — she even said it herself: 'well inventories is pretty, pretty straightforward.' Elevator at origin, second floor at destination, no packing. That is a bottom-of-range job quoted at the top of the range, on the phrase 'just to be on the safe side.'
No equivalents or plain-language anchor used. Nothing like the school-bus reference to make four and a half hours feel concrete against the inventory he just listed.
Traffic never mentioned as a variable despite a stated thirty-minute drive between addresses on a weekend.

Consolidation examples in the Save Your Ass speech were generic. 'Staging the boxes or the plastic tubs near the entry way' and 'disassemble the bed in advance' are good, but the specific list — kids' toys, garden tools, the loose stuff in drawers, photos off the walls — never came, and those are the items customers don't think of on their own.

No BOLDED-list framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. This matters more than usual on this call: she had already corrected two pieces of bad form data live (fifth floor was actually the fourth, and the email domain was wrong). Asking him to read the bolded list and reply with corrections is the cheap insurance against a third error nobody caught.
Hours and how to reach us never given — 'you can always call me back at this number' is a number, not hours.
Customer's name used twice, not three times. 'Michael' once at the stressor question and 'Mike' once inside the pricing block. Short of the standard on a ten-minute call.
Insurance was never explained as a concept. No 60c/lb industry baseline, no contrast, nothing the customer could use to compare Einstein against the next quote he gets.

The Sunday discount was pitched but never closed. She said 'if you guys are flexible, maybe you're interested in doing a Sunday instead to save a little what do you think?' and got 'I think that'd be possible we'll, we'll talk and see if that'll work' — then built the entire estimate on Sunday pricing without ever confirming Sunday actually works. The quote she is sending is priced for a date he has not agreed to.
top_strength: Amy's front half is the best-run intake in this week's sample, and the reason is that she treats the quote form as a draft to be verified rather than a fact. She read the whole record back — 'let me start with confirming your move date is September 26th which falls on a Saturday and you're moving out of a two bedroom apartment on the fifth floor with elevator. So from 8638. Uber road going to 1938 East Centra. Boulevard on the second floor' — and caught two errors in thirty seconds: the floor ('I guess I accidentally put it in as a fifth floor we're on the fourth floor') and the email domain ('Oh, no. It's supposed to be Gmail'). Two bad data points killed before they reached the estimate. Her box question is the model for the whole team: she didn't ask an open question, she gave an anchor — 'we normally see our account 25 to 35 boxes worth of items coming out of a two bedroom apartment. Would you say if you'll be in that range or do you have book collection shoe collection' — which is how you get a usable number instead of a shrug, and it worked (he reasoned his way to 'twenty or less'). She did the same with walk distance, splitting it deliberately into two measurable legs: 'let's divide into two. How far is the walk from your front door, going into the fourth floor elevator' and then 'once we get to the ground floor elevator going into the parking how far is that?' She got eight feet and twenty-to-thirty feet, real numbers instead of 'not far.' And she asked the stressor question by name, which almost nobody on this list did: 'Michael, what are you most worried about for this upcoming move or do you have any specific question that you would like me to answer during this call? Cause I wanna make sure we cover everything.' He handed her the whole sale — 'care, right, but also like cost and time' — and she immediately acted on the cost half by volunteering the cheaper Sunday tier unprompted rather than waiting to be pushed on price. She also delivered a genuine Save Your Ass close, the only full one this week: prep framed as money ('staging the boxes or the plastic tubs near the entry way or if you're able to disassemble the bed in advance even taking a hard load of the small pieces would really help you save time and of course money by the end of the day'), followed by 'Does that make sense so far?' That is the rubric's highest-value section, executed unprompted.
coaching_note: Estimate-accuracy flag, and this is the one to take to the bottom-4 review: Amy stated her own typical range for a two-bedroom apartment as three and a half to five and a half hours, then quoted four and a half to five and a half — the top half — with the words 'just to be on the safe side.' Read what she had in front of her when she said it. She had just called the inventory 'pretty, pretty straightforward.' Roughly a dozen furniture items and under twenty boxes. An elevator at origin, eight feet from the door. Second floor at destination. No packing services. The only real friction is a thirty-minute drive. That is a job that lives at the bottom of her range, and she quoted it at the top and told the customer she was doing it to be safe. This is the exact pattern behind the 45-46% number — the padding is not malice, it is risk aversion, and it costs twice: it inflates the quote the customer shops against, and when the movers finish in three and a half hours it teaches nobody anything because the 'win' was baked in. The fix is a sentence, not a system: 'Based on what you've described I'd budget three and a half to four and a half — the elevator and the short walks are doing a lot of work for you here.' If she is genuinely uncertain, name the specific uncertainty ('the sectional is my wildcard') instead of shifting the whole range up. Worth pulling the actual on this one if it books. Second priority: she gave away the three differentiators that answered the customer's own stated worries. He told her his concerns were 'care, right, but also like cost and time' — that is a customer literally reading out the cue cards for Meet Your Mover, No Worries Damage Coverage, and the On-Time Guarantee, and all three went unplayed. Her response to 'care' was 'Budget, really you know, money is the major factor' — she heard the cost half and dropped the care half entirely. The line she needed: 'Care is the one I can actually show you rather than promise. A few days before the move we email you a photo and a short bio of the movers who are coming, so you know exactly who's walking in your door. Every move carries our No Worries Damage Coverage, up to two thousand dollars to repair, replace, or reimburse any accidental damage — that's real coverage, not the sixty-cents-a-pound the industry hands you. And we give you an arrival window and an on-time guarantee: if we miss it, we start discounting.' That is ninety seconds against a customer who asked for it. Third, close the loop on the date. She priced the entire quote on Sunday after he said only 'that'd be possible we'll, we'll talk' — she is sending a quote for a date he hasn't agreed to, for a move he's still deciding on with a partner. The close should have been: 'Let's do this — since there's no deposit and nothing on a card, let me pencil in Sunday the 27th right now at the one-ninety-two rate so it's held while you two talk. If you decide on Saturday instead I'll just move it, and if you decide against us entirely you cancel with a text and it costs you nothing.' She said 'we don't require any deposits' — she just said it as a fact rather than using it as the tool that removes the risk from saying yes today. Fourth and smallest: put the name in three times and add the verification ask to the email handoff. She already caught two form errors on this call; asking him to read the bolded list and reply with corrections is how she catches the third one for free.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and responsive rather than scripted — she acknowledged what he said before moving on ('Oh, that's good, that's good,' 'Wonderful,' 'Amazing'), thanked him for asking how she was, and met the cost worry with real empathy ('money is the major factor and well the fact that you're moving that's very stressful itself. But no worries we're help, we're here to help you out'), though the name only came out twice and the care half of his concern went unacknowledged.
